03The reported problem

What Philips has experienced in the field

Summary of Philips’ safety notice

In radial-to-peripheral procedures, an unsuitable sheath or guide catheter can leave the wire and catheter without enough support.

The notice warns that continuing despite resistance could lead to tangling.

Philips Field Safety Notice 2024C06 · June 2025 · pp. 1 and 3View source ↗

Visions PV .014P, .014P RX and .018 · radial access to peripheral vessels

Philips’ precaution: use a guide sheath of appropriate length.

I modelled what that support changes in the wire.

Question·Background·Model·Test·Answer

07 One change at a time

Why the free length matters

The more wire is left free, the more often the catheter drags it back, with either hold.

  • Stays put. The catheter slides over it. In run 2, a point near the port moved 0.4 mm.
  • Partly dragged back.
  • Dragged back with the catheter. In run 1, that point moved 26.7 mm of the 27.5 mm pull.

The wire only swung all the way round the catheter when it was dragged back, at least partly.

How I sorted the runs

Every bar uses the same 59 sets of assumed inputs: drag in the RX lumen, wire stiffness, friction and a small starting kink. From bar to bar, only the free length or the hold changes.

For each run, I checked how much wire the port took up during the first 20 mm of pull (18 mm at 3 cm). Under a fifth of the pull: dragged back. Over four fifths: stays put. Anything in between: partly.

Runs 1 and 2 follow one point on the wire, about 5 mm before the port at the start. After 27.5 mm of pull it had moved 26.73 mm in run 1 and 0.36 mm in run 2. In run 2 it enters the RX lumen at 5.5 mm of pull. This follows one point, not the whole wire.

What the hold changes

The hold barely changes whether the wire gets dragged back. It changes how far a dragged wire then swings round the catheter.

Runs that swung a full turn round the catheter in the first 28 mm of pull, out of 59 at 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm: can roll 0, 0, 0, 17, 23, 41 and 50; held 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 20 and 27. Over the whole 100 mm pull, 16 held runs at 20 cm get there too, so the pull distance matters.

No run in which the wire stayed put swung a full turn, at any length or with either hold. A full turn describes the free wire’s angle round the catheter. It does not establish tangling or harm.

Why the length matters so much

The free wire acts like a slender column, and the catheter’s drag pushes on it. Held firmly at both ends, it buckles once the push passes 4π²EI/L². Double the free length and a quarter of the push is enough.

With my assumed drag and stiffness, the drag passes that load in 0, 0, 19, 47, 56, 58 and 59 of the 59 sets from 3 to 30 cm, close to where the wire starts getting dragged back. Firm ends give the highest load, so this is a comparison, not a limit.

The model reports 0.1700 N and 0.1501 N of added catheter pull from wire friction at the end of runs 1 and 2. But RX-lumen drag was set to 0.15 N, so getting roughly that force back is expected. It is not a measured device load. These numbers exclude other catheter resistance and are not the force at the wire clamp.

08 The next test

What I would do next

I’d start by measuring how the wire is held and how much the catheter drags on it.

With those values, I’d predict what happens at 3, 20 and 30 cm free.

In one pull, I’d record:

Wire movement

Track a point near the port.

Catheter pull force

Measure at the catheter hub.

Force at the wire clamp

Measure it separately from catheter pull.

If the results don’t match, I’d revise the model.

Proposed bench test. This study doesn’t establish a safe support length.

What I’d compare

I’d define the marker location, pull distance and comparison limits before testing. The model currently reports added catheter pull from wire friction, not total catheter pull or wire-clamp force. Those measurements need corresponding model outputs and a clear accounting of forces through the fixture before I can compare them.

Thank you
